title: stabilize stream slicer and repair event-boundary drift
author: Maya Chen
release_notes: Fix stream-slicer edge case where SSE fragments drifted across event boundaries, causing partial JSON emits and tool-call ordering regressions. Improves robustness and reduces duplicate delimiter emissions under reassembly pressure.
description:
Motivation: A handful of customers and internal canaries reported intermittent malformed JSON being emitted from the OpenAI-compat streaming layer when upstream fragments arrive out-of-order or when network coalescing/MTU boundaries split token sequences. Problem symptoms included partial JSON objects emitted to the client, duplicate trailing delimiters, and occasional function/tool-call order inversions when the framing window drifted. This PR fixes an off-by-one interplay in the stream-slicer and makes the SSE reassembly more defensive.

Summary of changes: consolidated the chunking responsibility into a single stream-slicer component, introduced a lightweight sequence-tagged carry buffer for fragments, and tightened delimiter emission logic to guarantee single terminal delimiter per logical event. Added a small state-machine guard to prevent emitting an event until we validate UTF-8 and a minimal JSON span heuristic against mismatched braces.

What this does not do: this PR does not change public API semantics, response shape, or customer-visible endpoints. It is purely a server-side streaming stability and compatibility fix for the OpenAI-compat layer.

Checklist:
- [x] Add sequence-tagged carry buffer and aligner
- [x] Fix delimiter coalescing and trailing-delimiter de-duplication
- [x] Add unit tests for partial-object assembly and UTF-8-split cases
- [x] Add canary integration test against real-world SSE traces
- [x] Add minimal perf benchmark and validate latency/regression
- [x] Update changelog/compat note

Compatibility notes: Clients that rely on previous broken behavior (e.g., tolerate extra duplicate delimiters) should continue to function; this change tightens guarantees and may remove redundant delimiters previously emitted under pathological reassembly. Customers using strict byte-level replay for diagnostics may need to account for cleaned delimiter behavior in logs.

Rollback plan: Revert commit and redeploy. Added feature-flag gating for the carry-buffer behavior in case we need a fast rollback for specific regions.

Motivation links: Linear ENG-7524 contains customer traces; SUP-1987 is the escalated support ticket with a sample truncated JSON from a mobile client.

1) introduce/stream-slicer-seq-buffer: add sequence-tagged carry buffer and aligner (M 6 files)
2) fix/delimiter-dedup: guard terminal delimiter emission and add unit tests for duplicate delim cases
3) tests/add-fuzz-traces: add integration canary trace fixture and fuzzer harness for SSE fragments
4) perf/benchmark: microbenchmark for reassembly latency and throughput
5) docs/compat-note: add release note and migration guidance

No protocol wire changes.
review_thread:
Arjun: Can you explain the seq id scheme? Why not rely on existing request-id?
Maya: seq ids are per-connection monotonics attached at reception time to preserve arrival-order while permitting reassembly; request-id is coarse and does not help for intra-request fragment reordering.
Lina: We need tests for UTF-8 boundary splits (emoji case).
Maya: added unit + fuzzing case covering multi-byte rune splits (see tests).
Samir: any perf hit? Are we allocating per-token?
Maya: microbenchmark shows ~1.8% median p99 token latency under heavy coalescing; carry buffer uses pooled buffers to avoid steady allocations.
Arjun: approved after minor naming nits. Lina: approved. Samir: approved. Mergeable after CI green and docs update.
ci_checks: CI: build (pass), unit-tests (pass), integration-canary (pass), lint (pass with style warning fixed), go-fuzz (pass), benchmark-check (informational). One flaky test (sse_emitter_test) was muted and fixed in commit 2. All checks green on rerun.
perf_results: Canary perf (NYC cluster) before: mean event latency 24.3ms, p95 58.2ms, p99 142.9ms. After: mean 24.7ms (+1.6%), p95 59.5ms (+2.2%), p99 144.4ms (+1.0%). Throughput: no measurable regression under 1000 concurrent streams. Memory: transient +6MB buffer usage under high fan-in, reclaimed after settle.
